newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Damaged wheat ship raises Sri Lanka pollution fear.
newsitem.headline: Damaged wheat ship raises Sri Lanka pollution fear.

text.p: A Greek-registered ship carrying wheat that was damaged by an underwater explosion in eastern Sri Lanka has raised environmental fears, maritime officials said on Thursday.

They said the Athena's engine room contained some 7,000 tonnes of water mixed with oil, and that the authorities had denied permission for the potentially hazardous mixture to be discharged into the sea.
They said the matter had been referred to Sri Lanka's Maritime Pollution Prevention Authority (MPPA), which was to decide what to do with the contaminated water.

"The engine room has some 7,000 tonnes of water and oil mixed with oil sludge at the bottom. If we let the ship discharge all that there could be serious problems to environment," MPPA Chairman Dhanapala Weerasekera told Reuters.

He said there was some contamination taking place now as the water moved in and out of the engine room with the tide, but added that there was no danger of large-scale pollution as most of the oil sludge had settled at the bottom.

The ship was anchored in the outer harbour at Trincomalee last week when the explosion occured. Naval officials said the blast was engineered by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels, who are fighting for an independent homeland in Sri Lanka's north and east.

In August last year, the rebels blasted a Philippines-registered cargo ship with an underwater device while it was loading mineral sand from a port 37 miles (60 km) north of Trincomalee. Some Sri Lankan crew members were wounded.
Trincomalee is known for its marine richness and whales, and officials fear that the water from Athena will affect marine life because of the oil content.
"One way to get rid of it is to discharge the water into another tanker and take it away. But we can't allow them to pump the water into the harbour," Weerasekera said.
Athena is carrying 52,000 tonnes Argentine wheat, which is still to be unloaded.
"We can't allow the unloading until the engine room is cleaned. It might upset the ship's balance," Weerasekera said.
